patient.name: Kwame Mensah
patient.setting: Emergency Department, then the sexual health clinic
patient.complaint: Two days of a painful, swollen right testicle
background: New female partner 3 weeks ago; no condoms

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' or 'most likely causative organism' with a painful scrotum: age and sexual history pick the organism, and onset, Prehn's sign and the cremasteric reflex separate it from torsion.

points: Kwame, 24: right testicle aching for **2 days**, getting worse.
**Unprotected sex** with a new partner 3 weeks ago.
No trauma; pain built up slowly, not in seconds.

steps.lead: Kwame has the textbook picture: one-sided, red, swollen, tender scrotum with fever and **dysuria**.
Under 35 with recent unprotected sex: think **Chlamydia** or **gonorrhoea** first.

visual.title: Age points to the organism
visual.label: Kwame 24
visual.caption: Under 35 = STI organisms; over 35 = urinary organisms. A recent catheter or UTI also points to urinary bugs.

points: Lifting the testis **eases** the pain (Prehn's sign).
Testis lies normally; cremasteric reflex present.
No hard lump; swelling does not transilluminate.

steps.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
steps.r: Gradual painful swelling, fever, dysuria and pain eased by lifting the testis fit **epididymo-orchitis**. Torsion is sudden and elevation does not help.

steps.lead: Kwame's infection probably started in the **epididymis** and is spreading into the testis: epididymo-orchitis.

visual.title: How the pain builds
visual.caption: Torsion hits in minutes; epididymo-orchitis builds over hours to days.

steps.lead: Kwame's positive **Prehn's sign** argues against torsion. Mumps orchitis would follow a swollen parotid by 4 to 8 days.

steps.text: A sudden painful testis in a teenager is **torsion until proven otherwise**. Do not let an epididymitis label delay a surgical review.

steps.lead: Kwame needs to hear why treatment matters: untreated infection risks **abscess**, chronic pain and infertility.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (urine dipstick), then the test that matches the likely organism (first-void NAAT under 35, MSU culture over 35), and scrotal ultrasound to exclude torsion.

steps.q: Which test is done first in the ED?
steps.r: The **urine dipstick** is the initial test: it shows leucocytes and nitrites and supports infection.

steps.lead: Kwame is under 35 with STI risk, so after the dipstick he needs a **first-void urine NAAT** for chlamydia and gonorrhoea.

steps.title: Kwame's results
steps.text: Leucocytes without nitrites fits an STI urethritis rather than a typical E. coli UTI. The NAAT confirms chlamydia.
Match the test to the age: **under 35 = first-void urine NAAT** (or urethral swab); **over 35 = MSU** for microscopy and culture.

points: The registrar is fairly sure, but the pain is severe.
Ultrasound: swollen, hyperaemic epididymis; normal testicular blood flow.

steps.lead: Kwame's ultrasound shows **increased** flow to the epididymis. Torsion would show reduced or absent flow to the testis.

steps.text: Mumps serology is not the first test in a sexually active man with dysuria. Think STI first, mumps only with parotid swelling.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': IM ceftriaxone plus oral doxycycline for an STI cause, oral ofloxacin for a urinary cause, and supportive care for mumps orchitis.

steps.q: Which antibiotic plan is right for Kwame?
steps.r: Under 35 with STI risk: **IM ceftriaxone** (gonorrhoea) **plus doxycycline** (chlamydia), started before results return.

steps.lead: Kwame gets a **single IM ceftriaxone** dose and **doxycycline twice daily for 2 weeks**, covering both gonorrhoea and chlamydia.

steps.title: Which regimen?
head: Cause
Typical patient
Treatment
rows: IM ceftriaxone once + oral doxycycline 2 weeks

steps.lead: Kwame also needs **analgesia, fluids and scrotal support**. He was vaccinated, so mumps is unlikely.

visual.title: Response to treatment
visual.caption: Fever settles in days; swelling can take weeks. No improvement in 3 days means reassess for abscess.

steps.text: An STI cause means **partner notification** and a full sexual health screen; he should avoid sex until he and his partner are treated.
Ofloxacin alone is the urinary regimen. In a young man with STI risk it misses **gonorrhoea**, so it is the wrong answer.

science.exam: Science questions ask how infection reaches the epididymis (retrograde spread), why mumps causes orchitis (haematogenous) and why Prehn's sign works.

steps.lead: Kwame's chlamydia travelled **backwards** from the urethra up the vas deferens to the epididymis.

steps.title: Retrograde spread
steps.caption: In older men, BPH causes stasis, which seeds urinary organisms the same way.

steps.lead: If Kwame had been unvaccinated with swollen parotids, the virus would have reached the testis through the **blood**.

steps.q: Why did lifting Kwame's testis ease his pain?
o: It reduces venous congestion of the inflamed testis
steps.r: Elevation helps an oedematous, inflamed testis drain. In torsion the pedicle is twisted, so it does not help.

steps.lead: Kwame's positive Prehn's sign makes sense: his testis is inflamed, not ischaemic.

mcq.q: Which organisms most commonly cause epididymo-orchitis in men under 35?
Which organism is most common in men over 35?
mcq.r: Over 35, **urinary pathogens** such as E. coli dominate.

o: Pain worse on lifting the testis
Pain relieved by lifting the testis
mcq.r: Relief on elevation suggests **epididymitis** rather than torsion.

mcq.q: How long after parotid swelling does mumps orchitis typically appear?
Which is a complication of epididymo-orchitis?
What is the initial test in suspected epididymo-orchitis?
Which test is used when an STI cause is suspected?
mcq.r: **NAAT** on first-void urine or a urethral swab.

mcq.q: What is first-line treatment for STI-related epididymitis?
mcq.r: Single IM ceftriaxone plus **doxycycline twice daily for 2 weeks**.

mcq.q: How does bacterial infection usually reach the epididymis?
o: Retrograde spread along the vas deferens
mcq.r: Pathogens ascend **from the urethra or bladder** via the vas.

technique.stem: A 27 year old man has a 3 day history of increasing pain and swelling of his left testis and burning on passing urine. He has had two new sexual partners this month. His temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg. The left epididymis is swollen and tender. The pain eases when the testis is elevated. The cremasteric reflex is present.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about a painful scrotum: first decide infection vs torsion.

clues: pain eases when the testis is elevated
steps.x: Gradual onset, dysuria, STI risk, fever, positive Prehn's sign and a present reflex all point away from torsion.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Infection of the epididymis spreading to the testis: **epididymo-orchitis**.

elim: A hernia gives a groin swelling you cannot get above, with obstructive symptoms, not dysuria.
Mumps follows parotid swelling and is not linked to dysuria or new partners.
Torsion is sudden, the reflex is absent and elevation does not ease pain.
A tumour is a painless, hard, craggy lump.

steps.x: **A. Epididymo-orchitis.** Rule: gradual + dysuria + Prehn's positive = infection; sudden + absent reflex = torsion.

technique.stem: A 61 year old man has a 2 day history of a painful, swollen right testis. He had a urinary catheter removed a week ago after a hip replacement. He has a single long-term partner. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 140/84 mmHg. Urine dipstick shows leucocytes and nitrites.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to identify the causative organism?

steps.x: An investigation question asking for the organism: decide STI or urinary first.

clues: urinary catheter removed a week ago
steps.x: Over 35, recent catheter, low STI risk and nitrites: a urinary organism such as E. coli.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Urinary organism = **MSU for microscopy and culture**.

elim: NAAT looks for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, which are unlikely here.
AFP is a testicular tumour marker, not an infection test.
Mumps is a young unvaccinated man's disease after parotitis.
Biopsy is never used to diagnose infection and risks spread.

steps.x: **B. Mid-stream urine microscopy and culture.** Rule: over 35 = MSU; under 35 = NAAT.

technique.stem: A 20 year old man has a 2 day history of a painful, swollen left testis and urethral discharge. He had unprotected sex with a new partner 10 days ago. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 90 bpm and BP 122/74 mmHg. Prehn's sign is positive. Scrotal ultrasound shows normal testicular blood flow. NAAT results are awaited.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

steps.x: Initial management: start treatment that covers the likely organisms before the results are back.

clues: unprotected sex with a new partner
steps.x: Young man with an STI picture, torsion excluded: cover both gonorrhoea and chlamydia now.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IM ceftriaxone single dose plus doxycycline twice daily for 2 weeks.**

elim: Amoxicillin covers neither chlamydia nor gonorrhoea reliably.
Ofloxacin is the urinary-organism regimen and misses gonorrhoea.
Bacterial infection needs antibiotics; supportive care alone is for mumps.
Ultrasound has excluded torsion.

steps.x: **A. IM ceftriaxone plus oral doxycycline.** Treat empirically; do not wait for NAAT.

technique.stem: A 25 year old man has a 2 day history of a painful, swollen right testis. When the doctor gently lifts the testis, his pain is clearly reduced. Ultrasound shows an enlarged, oedematous epididymis with increased blood flow.
technique.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the reduction in pain?
o: Increased arterial inflow to the testis
Reduced venous congestion of the inflamed tissue

steps.x: A mechanism question explaining a sign in the vignette: Prehn's sign.
An inflamed, oedematous epididymis with no torsion: lifting helps it drain.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Elevation reduces **venous congestion** and so the pain.

elim: Elevation does not increase arterial inflow.
The cremaster is not the source of the pain.
Elevation does not stretch this nerve, and it does not explain relief.
There is no torsion here; flow is increased.

steps.x: **B. Reduced venous congestion.** In torsion the pedicle is twisted, so elevation cannot help.

practice.stem: A 23 year old man has a 2 day history of gradually worsening pain and swelling in his right testis. He has dysuria. He had unprotected sex with a new partner 3 weeks ago. His temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 100 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg. The right hemiscrotum is red and the epididymis is tender. Lifting the testis relieves the pain.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Gradual unilateral scrotal pain with fever, dysuria and a positive Prehn's sign is epididymo-orchitis. Torsion is sudden and not eased by elevation.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a painful scrotum: infection or torsion?

clues: Lifting the testis relieves the pain
steps.x: Gradual, febrile, dysuria, STI risk, positive Prehn's sign.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Epididymo-orchitis.**

elim: A cyst is painless, fluctuant and separate from the testis.
Torsion is sudden and elevation does not relieve the pain.
A tumour is painless and hard.
A varicocele is a painless 'bag of worms', usually left-sided.

steps.x: **B. Epididymo-orchitis.**

practice.stem: A 26 year old man has a 3 day history of a painful, swollen left testis and a clear urethral discharge. He has had several casual partners and rarely uses condoms. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 130/78 mmHg. The left epididymis is swollen and tender.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Under 35 with STI risk, chlamydia (and gonorrhoea) are the most common causes. E. coli is the over-35 urinary organism.

steps.x: Organism question: age and sexual history decide it.
Under 35 with STI risk and a clear discharge.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The commonest STI cause: **Chlamydia trachomatis**.

elim: E. coli is the commonest cause over 35 or with UTI.
Mumps follows parotitis in unvaccinated men.
Staph is not a typical cause of epididymitis.
Syphilis causes a painless chancre, not epididymitis.

steps.x: **A. Chlamydia trachomatis.**

practice.stem: A 66 year old man has a 2 day history of a painful, swollen right testis. He has a long history of a weak urinary stream and nocturia. He had a urinary catheter for 3 days last week. His temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 142/86 mmHg. Urine dipstick shows nitrites and leucocytes.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Over 35, after catheterisation and with BPH, a urinary pathogen such as E. coli is most likely.

steps.x: Organism question in an older man.
Over 35, probable BPH with stasis, recent catheter, nitrite-positive urine.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A urinary organism: **E. coli**.

elim: Chlamydia is the under-35 STI organism.
Mumps orchitis follows parotitis in unvaccinated men.
TB epididymitis is rare and chronic, often with a beaded vas.
Gonorrhoea is an STI organism in younger men.

steps.x: **B. Escherichia coli.**

practice.stem: A 19 year old man has a 1 day history of a painful, swollen left testis. A week ago he had fever and painful swelling in front of both ears. He was not vaccinated as a child. He has never been sexually active. His temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Orchitis 4 to 8 days after parotid swelling in an unvaccinated young man is mumps. No sexual activity rules out gonorrhoea.

steps.x: Diagnosis: link the earlier illness to the testis.

clues: swelling in front of both ears
steps.x: Parotitis about a week ago in an unvaccinated young man, then orchitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Mumps orchitis.**

elim: He has never been sexually active.
EBV gives sore throat and lymphadenopathy, not orchitis after parotitis.
Torsion is sudden and has no link to parotitis.
A tumour is painless and gradual.

steps.x: **C. Mumps orchitis.** Orchitis 4 to 8 days after parotitis.

practice.stem: A 28 year old man has a 2 day history of increasing right scrotal pain and fever. He had unprotected sex 2 weeks ago. His temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg. The right epididymis is swollen and tender posteriorly. The testis lies normally.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on further examination?
o: High-riding testis with a horizontal lie
Pain relieved by elevating the testis
practice.e: Prehn's sign (pain relieved by elevation) supports epididymo-orchitis. A high-riding testis and absent reflex point to torsion.

steps.x: A 'most likely finding' question: predict the sign from the diagnosis.
This is epididymo-orchitis, so the classic sign is Prehn's.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Pain relieved by elevating the testis** (positive Prehn's sign).

elim: That suggests torsion.
That suggests a tumour.
That is the torsion picture.
That is a hydrocele or cyst.

steps.x: **D. Pain relieved by elevating the testis.** The other options are torsion, tumour or hydrocele signs.

practice.stem: A 32 year old man and his partner have been trying to conceive for 2 years. At 17 he was unvaccinated and had painful swelling of both testes a week after swelling of his parotid glands. Both testes are now small and soft. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his subfertility?
practice.e: Bilateral mumps orchitis can cause testicular atrophy and subfertility, shown by low sperm count and raised FSH.

steps.x: A cause question: join the past history to the present problem.

clues: a week after swelling of his parotid glands
steps.x: Bilateral orchitis after parotitis, now atrophic testes and low sperm count.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Bilateral mumps orchitis** causing testicular atrophy.

elim: There is no history of steroid use.
There is no history of undescended testes.
Klinefelter causes lifelong small testes, not a clear post-infective history.
A varicocele is a palpable 'bag of worms' and does not shrink both testes like this.

steps.x: **B. Bilateral mumps orchitis.** Bilateral orchitis carries the subfertility risk.

practice.stem: A 22 year old man has a 2 day history of a painful, swollen left testis and dysuria. He has a new sexual partner. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg. Urine dipstick shows leucocytes but no nitrites. Testicular blood flow on ultrasound is normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

practice.stem: A 30 year old man has a 12 hour history of right testicular pain and swelling. The pain began gradually. He has mild dysuria. practice.e: Scrotal ultrasound with Doppler shows testicular blood flow and excludes torsion. Urine tests identify the organism but cannot exclude torsion.

practice.stem: A 63 year old man has a 2 day history of a painful, swollen left testis following a urinary tract infection. He is in a long-term monogamous relationship. practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Epididymo-orchitis from a urinary pathogen is treated with oral ofloxacin for 14 days. Ceftriaxone plus doxycycline is the STI regimen.

practice.stem: A 20 year old unvaccinated man has a painful, swollen right testis 5 days after developing bilateral parotid swelling. He is not sexually active. His temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 122/70 mmHg. Ultrasound shows an enlarged testis with increased blood flow. Urine dipstick is negative.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Mumps orchitis is managed supportively with rest, analgesia and scrotal elevation; antibiotics do not help. MMR prevents it.

practice.stem: A 25 year old man has epididymo-orchitis. First-void urine NAAT is positive for Chlamydia trachomatis. Ten days earlier he had a urethral discharge and dysuria. Ultrasound shows a swollen epididymis with inflammation extending into the testis.
practice.q: Which is the most likely route by which infection reached the epididymis?
o: Direct spread from the inguinal canal
Retrograde spread along the vas deferens
Spread from the overlying scrotal skin
practice.e: Bacteria ascend from the urethra or bladder along the vas deferens to the epididymis, then spread into the testis. Haematogenous spread is mumps.

steps.x: A mechanism question: how does a urethral infection reach the epididymis?

clues: Ten days earlier he had a urethral discharge
steps.x: Urethritis first, then epididymitis, then the testis.

steps.x: **Retrograde spread** up the vas deferens, then contiguous spread into the testis.

elim: The inguinal canal is not a route of infection here.
That is how mumps reaches the testis.
Lymphatics are not the usual route.
There is no skin infection.

steps.x: **D. Retrograde spread along the vas deferens.**

glossary.epididymis: The coiled tube behind the testis that stores and carries sperm.
glossary.epididymitis: Inflammation of the epididymis, usually from infection.
glossary.epididymo-orchitis: Infection and inflammation of both the epididymis and the testis.
glossary.testicular torsion: Twisting of the spermatic cord cutting off the testis's blood supply; a surgical emergency.
glossary.Prehn's sign: Pain relieved by lifting the testis; supports epididymitis rather than torsion.
glossary.cremasteric reflex: Stroking the inner thigh makes the testis rise; usually absent in torsion.
glossary.spermatic cord: The bundle carrying the vas deferens, testicular vessels and nerves.
glossary.vas deferens: The duct carrying sperm from the epididymis to the urethra.
glossary.Chlamydia trachomatis: A common sexually transmitted bacterium; a leading cause of epididymitis under 35.
glossary.Neisseria gonorrhoeae: The bacterium causing gonorrhoea; an STI cause of epididymitis.
glossary.E. coli: Escherichia coli: a gut bacterium that is the commonest urinary pathogen.
glossary.Klebsiella: A Gram-negative bacterium that causes urinary and other infections.
glossary.mumps: A paramyxovirus infection causing parotid swelling; can spread to the testis.
glossary.parotitis: Inflammation and swelling of the parotid salivary glands.
glossary.MMR: The measles, mumps and rubella vaccine.
glossary.NAAT: Nucleic acid amplification test: a very sensitive DNA test for chlamydia and gonorrhoea.
glossary.first-void urine: The first part of the urine stream, which carries urethral organisms for NAAT.
glossary.MSU: Mid-stream urine sample for microscopy and culture.
glossary.urine dipstick: A quick strip test for leucocytes, nitrites, blood and protein in urine.
glossary.nitrites: Made by many Gram-negative bacteria such as E. coli; a positive dipstick suggests UTI.
glossary.dysuria: Pain or burning on passing urine.
glossary.ceftriaxone: A third-generation cephalosporin given IM to treat gonorrhoea.
glossary.doxycycline: A tetracycline antibiotic that treats chlamydia.
glossary.ofloxacin: A fluoroquinolone antibiotic used for urinary-organism epididymitis.
glossary.scrotal ultrasound: Imaging of the scrotum; Doppler shows testicular blood flow to exclude torsion.
glossary.retrograde spread: Infection travelling backwards up a duct, here from urethra to epididymis.
glossary.hydrocele: Fluid around the testis giving a soft swelling that transilluminates.
glossary.partner notification: Informing and treating sexual partners of someone with an STI.
